li.a: SOA Watch: Summary of 1993 UN Truth Commission Report on El Salvador
Unfinished Sentences: The Massacre of El Mozote: 36 Years of Struggles for Truth and Justice
CEJIL: Amnesty law must not prevent investigation of gross human rights violations in El Salvador
El Salvador Perspectives: Salvadoran judge reopens case of El Mozote massacre
El Salvador Perspectives: The 40 year quest for justice

content.p: In the second week of December 1981, soldiers of the Salvadoran army moved through the hamlets of Morazán, a department in the northeast of El Salvador, and killed the people they found there. The worst of it happened in El Mozote, a village where women and children gathered in a church building were shot and burned, according to Unfinished Sentences, which describes the killings as the largest massacre in contemporary Latin American history.

Salvadoran authorities denied it. When a criminal case was opened in 1990 it was archived three years later under an amnesty law. The legal fight over El Mozote continued for more than three decades after that.

The killings were part of a military operation the army called "Operation Rescue". The Salvadoran army units that carried them out were led principally by the Atlacatl Battalion, which Unfinished Sentences describes as a US-trained counterinsurgency unit. CEJIL, which later represented the victims before the Inter-American Court, dates the killings to 9 to 13 December 1981 and says the army tortured many of its victims. Unfinished Sentences gives the days as 10 to 13 December, and places the scorched-earth killings in El Mozote and the surrounding towns.

The soldiers did not only kill people in El Mozote. CEJIL lists seven hamlets and villages in the municipality of Meanguera where people were killed, El Mozote among them. The killings also drove hundreds of people from their homes.

The first accounts reached the outside world in January 1982. Unfinished Sentences records that two newspapers, The New York Times and The Washington Post, ran reports by Raymond Bonner and Alma Guillermoprieto on 27 January 1982, based on a January visit to the site and on the testimony of Rufina Amaya, a survivor. The reports drew international attention to the atrocity.

Official denial followed. Unfinished Sentences records that Salvadoran authorities denied the massacre and kept silent, and that in 1989 Tutela Legal, the human rights office of the Archdiocese of San Salvador, opened its own investigation. Tutela Legal later represented the victims.

The first criminal complaint was filed on 26 October 1990 before the court in San Francisco Gotera. It was brought by Pedro Chicas, a survivor of the La Joya massacre, with Tutela Legal's help. Unfinished Sentences says that the complaint opened the official criminal investigation into El Mozote.

The investigation stalled almost at once. On 8 May 1991, according to Unfinished Sentences, the presiding judge, Federico Portillo Campos, suspended the taking of witness testimony, which left hundreds of witnesses and relatives of victims unable to testify. When forensic anthropologists of the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team asked to take part in digging up the sites, the judge said he could not decide without instructions from the president of the Supreme Court, Mauricio Castro. El Salvador Perspectives also reports that the same judge later conceded he had been given orders by senior officials to shut the case.

Tutela Legal published the first results of its own investigation on 12 November 1991. Unfinished Sentences says the report established the chronology of the massacre and showed that several army units took part, including the Atlacatl Battalion, the Air Force, an artillery brigade, the Third Infantry Brigade of San Miguel and the commando training centre at San Francisco Gotera. Within days, the judge and the district attorney raised a rumour about landmines in the area, which Unfinished Sentences says stalled the case further.

Exhumations began at the convent beside the town church on 13 October 1992, and remains were examined in November of that year. The forensic work was done by the Argentine team together with Salvadoran institutions.

The United Nations-backed Commission on the Truth for El Salvador was not a court. It had six months under the peace accords to examine the worst abuses of the war by all sides, the impunity of the military and security forces, and to recommend reforms. It received testimony from 2,000 sources relating to 7,000 victims, according to the SOA Watch summary of its report. The Commission presented its El Mozote findings to the UN Secretary-General on 15 March 1993.

The summary says the Commission found that the army killed more than 200 people in El Mozote, including women and children. It named Col. Domingo Monterrosa Barrios, the former Atlacatl commander, as the officer in charge of the massacre, and noted that he had died. It also cited Col. Natividad de Jesús Cáceres Cabrera, who was a major at the time, and found that the Supreme Court president, Mauricio Gutiérrez Castro, had improperly interfered in the judicial investigation. The Commission called for more than 40 military personnel to be removed from the armed forces or from public office. Unfinished Sentences says the report confirmed the earlier findings of Tutela Legal and recommended that the state carry out a serious investigation.

The report had little effect on the courts. In 1993 a General Amnesty Law was passed for the Consolidation of Peace. CEJIL says the case was archived in September 1993 under that law, which exempted those responsible for the crimes of the war from prosecution. Unfinished Sentences describes the amnesty as one of the main barriers to justice.

The Salvadoran state did not reopen the case for many years. In January 2012 it accepted responsibility for the events of the massacre and promised reparations, according to CEJIL. El Salvador Perspectives reports that in April 2015 government forensic investigators dug up the remains of a family and two dozen other victims, but the investigation then stalled because of the 1993 decision to archive the case.

On Monday 10 December 2012, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued its judgment in the case "The Massacres at El Mozote and Neighboring Locations". The date was International Human Rights Day and the 31st anniversary of the killings. CEJIL, which represented the victims with Tutela Legal, says it was the first time the highest tribunal in the Americas had ruled that El Salvador's amnesty law was incompatible with the American Convention on Human Rights. The judgment condemned El Salvador and held that the amnesty could not be used to block investigation of human rights violations committed during the armed conflict.

CEJIL's lawyers said the judgment could not be appealed and that El Salvador was bound to comply with it within the time the court set. The organisation's press release also described El Mozote as the largest massacre in Latin America and said that the killings in the region of six villages had led to hundreds of forced displacements. Tutela Legal welcomed the judgment but warned that the court's ruling should be viewed with caution.

The legal position changed in July 2016, when the Supreme Court overturned the amnesty law, according to El Salvador Perspectives. In 2016 the Second Court of First Instance in San Francisco Gotera reopened the investigation. The request came from the Association to Promote Human Rights of El Mozote, the Center for Justice and International Law and Maria Julia Hernández's legal defence agency, and the judge, Jorge Guzmán Urquilla, accepted it.

Unfinished Sentences says that 18 former high-ranking military officers, including former defence minister José Guillermo García Merino, face charges of murder, aggravated rape and acts of terrorism. Dozens of survivors and eyewitnesses have testified in court, some of them for the first time. These officers are accused; no court had convicted any of them when the pages were written.

El Salvador Perspectives notes that the 2016 ruling upset both former military men and the governing party, which grew out of the FMLN. The Tutela Legal lawyer Ovidio González said the ruling let the victims return to the judge and argue that the 1993 decision to close the case was illegal.

The death toll is the least settled part of the record. The Truth Commission summary gives more than 200 people killed in El Mozote itself. Unfinished Sentences gives at least 978 across El Mozote and the surrounding areas. CEJIL puts the total at around 1,000 across at least six villages. Each figure comes from a different source, and the difference is partly one of geography: a count of one village is not a count of the whole operation.

The dates also differ. The SOA Watch summary of the Truth Commission report gives the year as 1980, while the other pages give December 1981. The survivor named Pedro Chicas is given with different surnames on different pages. None of these differences changes the central account, but readers should weigh each figure by its source.
